prompt: Two 3x3 convolutions in a row: how large a patch of the input does one value at the end depend on?
hint: Each value of the first output saw a 3 by 3 patch.

choices.text: 3 by 3, the size of each filter
choices.why: That is what one layer sees. The second layer reads 3 by 3 values that each saw 3 by 3 pixels, so the patch grows.

choices.text: 5 by 5
choices.why: Right. `stack.py` lit one pixel and counted 25 outputs, the same as one 5x5 filter.

choices.text: 6 by 6, the two sizes added
choices.why: Each extra 3x3 layer adds one pixel on every side, two in width, not three.

choices.text: 9 by 9, the two sizes multiplied
choices.why: The patches overlap; three layers reach 7 by 7, so two cannot reach 9 by 9.

prompt: Why did VGG prefer two 3x3 convolutions to one 5x5 with the same receptive field?
hint: Compare the parameter counts, and what sits between the two layers.

choices.text: A 3x3 filter is faster on a graphics card whatever the count
choices.why: Speed per filter was not the argument; the count and the extra non-linearity were.

choices.text: Two layers see a larger patch than one 5x5
choices.why: They see the same 25 pixels, which is why the comparison is fair.

choices.text: Fewer weights, and a ReLU between them
choices.why: Right: 73,856 against 102,464 at 64 channels, and the ReLU lets the pair compute what one linear filter cannot.

choices.text: A 5x5 filter cannot be trained with backpropagation
choices.why: Any filter size trains; AlexNet's first layer was 11x11.

prompt: A colleague wants to shrink a VGG-16 to fit a phone and starts by removing two of its 13 convolutions. Going by the counts in this lesson, why will that barely help?
hint: Where do most of VGG-16's parameters sit?

choices.text: Convolutions share weights across the image, so they hold none
choices.why: They share them, but they still hold 14,714,688 between them.

choices.text: Removing layers makes the network train worse
choices.why: That may or may not be so, but it is not about size.

choices.text: The phone runs convolutions on dedicated hardware
choices.why: Hardware changes speed, not the number of weights to store.

choices.text: Nearly all the weight is in the dense head
choices.why: Right: 123,642,856 of 138,357,544 are in the three dense layers. Replacing that head with an average and one small layer is what ResNet did.

prompt: What makes the degradation problem different from overfitting?
hint: Which set does the deeper network do worse on?

choices.text: The deeper network is worse on its own training data
choices.why: Right. Overfitting is good on training and bad on validation; here training itself fails.

choices.text: Only the validation loss rises
choices.why: That is overfitting's signature, the one this is not.

choices.text: It happens only with small data sets
choices.why: The ResNet paper saw it on ImageNet's million images.

choices.text: It goes away with dropout
choices.why: Dropout fights overfitting; it gives a network that cannot fit its training set nothing.

prompt: In `depth.py`, the 20-layer plain network's training loss sits at 2.30 for twenty epochs. What does that number mean on the digits?
hint: What is the cross-entropy of a network that is equally unsure of all ten classes?

choices.text: The network has learnt the digits and is overfitting
choices.why: An overfitting network has a training loss near zero, not stuck high.

choices.text: It gives every digit the same probability
choices.why: Right: minus the log of 1/10 is about 2.30. The network learnt nothing, and its accuracy is a fixed guess.

choices.text: The rate is too high
choices.why: A diverging loss climbs or turns into nan; this one does not move.

choices.text: The network needs more epochs, since the loss falls slowly
choices.why: It does not fall slowly; it does not fall, while the 8-layer network falls fast.

prompt: A deeper network can always copy a shallower one by making its extra layers pass their input through. Given that, what does a deeper plain network with a WORSE training loss tell you?
hint: A better solution exists. Who failed to find it?

choices.text: Twenty layers are too few parameters for the digits
choices.why: The 20-layer network has eight times the parameters of the 4-layer one, which trains.

choices.text: The data needs augmenting
choices.why: Augmentation helps generalisation, and the failure here is on the training set itself.

choices.text: The optimiser cannot reach a solution that exists
choices.why: Right. The weights for at least the shallow network's loss exist inside the deep one; training did not find them.

choices.text: The test set is harder than the training set
choices.why: The test set was never used, and the training loss is the one that is worse.

prompt: What does the `Residual` class of `deep.py` change about the `Plain` block?
hint: Compare the two `forward` methods.

choices.text: It adds a third convolution
choices.why: It inherits the same two convolutions and nothing else.

choices.text: It adds the input to the output of the second convolution
choices.why: Right: `x +` before the last ReLU, and the same parameters.

choices.text: It doubles the channels
choices.why: The width stays 16 throughout, which is why `x` and `f(x)` can be added.

choices.text: It removes the ReLU that sits between the two convolutions of the block
choices.why: That ReLU is still there; the skip is the only change.

prompt: `grads.py` shows the first block of the plain 20-layer network getting a gradient more than a million times smaller than the last. Why does the residual one not?
hint: Differentiate `x + f(x)` with respect to `x`.

choices.text: Its weights were started larger
choices.why: Both networks were built from the same seed with the same weights.

choices.text: It uses a different loss
choices.why: Both use cross-entropy on the same batch.

choices.text: The addition passes the gradient back unchanged
choices.why: Right: the derivative of `x + f(x)` is 1 plus what `f` adds, so there is a path where nothing is multiplied away.

choices.text: Its gradients are clipped to a fixed size
choices.why: Nothing in `grads.py` clips anything; it only measures.

prompt: A residual block computes `relu(x + f(x))`. If its convolutions learn nothing useful and `f(x)` stays near zero, the block outputs roughly its ___, which is why extra blocks cannot make things much worse.
hint: What is left of `x + f(x)` when `f(x)` is 0?

prompt: Between one stage of ResNet-18 and the next, what happens to the image and to the channels?
hint: Read the shapes `resnet.py` printed.

choices.text: Both halve
choices.why: The channels go up, from 64 to 128 to 256 to 512.

choices.text: The side halves and the channels double
choices.why: Right: 56, 28, 14, 7 on the side, and 64 up to 512 channels.

choices.text: The image stays 224 by 224 and the channels double
choices.why: The stem has already taken it to 56 by 56 before the first stage.

choices.text: Nothing changes: only the weights differ between stages
choices.why: The printed shapes change at every stage after the first.

prompt: In the printed block `layer2[0]`, what is `downsample` for?
hint: `f(x)` came out with 128 channels at 28 by 28. What shape is `x`?

choices.text: It shrinks the image before the block's convolutions
choices.why: The block's own path shrinks it, with `stride=(2, 2)` on `conv1`; `downsample` sits on the skip.

choices.text: It brings `x` to the shape of `f(x)`, ready for the addition
choices.why: Right: a 1x1 convolution with stride 2 takes 64 channels at 56 by 56 to 128 at 28 by 28.

choices.text: It replaces batch normalisation in the first block
choices.why: The block still has `bn1` and `bn2`, and `downsample` has a `BatchNorm2d` of its own.

choices.text: It is the classifier
choices.why: The classifier is `fc`, after the last stage.

prompt: Put in order what an image passes through in torchvision's ResNet-18, from the input to the class scores.
hint: The stem first, the head last.

prompt: What does a depthwise convolution leave out that a full convolution does?
hint: `groups=32` puts each channel in a group of its own.

choices.text: Looking at a neighbourhood of pixels
choices.why: That is the half it keeps: each channel still gets a 3x3 filter.

choices.text: Mixing the channels
choices.why: Right. Each channel is filtered alone, and the 1x1 pointwise convolution after it does the mixing.

choices.text: Padding the edges of the image
choices.why: `separable.py` gives it `padding=1`, like the full one.

choices.text: The activation after the filter
choices.why: Activations are separate layers in both cases.

prompt: A depthwise separable convolution goes from 64 channels to 128 with a 3x3 depthwise filter, and neither part has a bias. How many parameters does it have?
hint: Depthwise: 3 × 3 per input channel. Pointwise: input channels times output channels.

prompt: `scaling.py` printed EfficientNet-B0 to B7. What does compound scaling grow from one to the next?
hint: Look at which columns change between B0 and B7.

choices.text: Only the number of blocks
choices.why: The blocks grow, but so do the width and the image.

choices.text: Only the image size, with the network fixed
choices.why: The parameters go from 5,288,548 to 66,347,960, so the network grows too.

choices.text: Depth, width and image size together
choices.why: Right: 16 to 55 blocks, 320 to 640 channels, 224 to 600 pixels.

choices.text: The number of classes
choices.why: All eight are ImageNet models with the same 1,000 classes.

prompt: EfficientNet-B0 needs less than a tenth of ResNet-50's operations per image. Why might it still not run ten times faster on a graphics card?
hint: What does a depthwise convolution do per byte it reads?

choices.text: Depthwise layers do little arithmetic per byte they read
choices.why: Right. Time depends on moving data as well as on arithmetic, so operations are a guide, not a stopwatch.

choices.text: The GFLOPs on the card were counted for a larger image than ResNet-50's
choices.why: Both rows are for 224 by 224, the image column says so.

choices.text: EfficientNet has more parameters to load
choices.why: It has about a fifth of ResNet-50's.

choices.text: Graphics cards cannot run depthwise convolutions
choices.why: They run them; they just run them less efficiently than dense ones.

prompt: You must classify 28 by 28 grey sketches into 20 classes, with 2,000 training images and no pretrained weights for anything like them. Going by this lesson, what is a sensible first model?
hint: Think about what ResNet-18's stem does to a small image.

choices.text: EfficientNet-B7, the most accurate on ImageNet
choices.why: It was scaled for 600 by 600 photographs and has 66,347,960 parameters for 2,000 images.

choices.text: A small CNN of your own, sized for 28 by 28
choices.why: Right. On the 8 by 8 digits, lesson 11's 38,282-parameter network beat ResNet-18 at about 290 times the size.

choices.text: VGG-16, because its dense head can learn 20 classes
choices.why: Any head learns 20 classes; VGG's costs over a hundred million parameters to do it.

choices.text: ResNet-50 with its stem unchanged
choices.why: The stem divides the side by four before the first block, leaving 7 by 7 from 28 by 28, and expects three colour channels.

prompt: Match each architecture with the change it is remembered for.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: each block's input added to its output
depth, width and image size scaled together

right_distractors: filters of several sizes side by side

prompt: Which of these are true of the residual networks in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are true.

choices.text: A residual block has the same parameters as the plain block it extends
choices.why: True: `Residual` inherits both convolutions from `Plain`, and the counts match line for line.

choices.text: The skip connection holds weights of its own in every block
choices.why: In `deep.py` it holds none, and in ResNet-18 only the first block of a stage has a 1x1 `downsample`.

choices.text: At 20 layers, the residual network trained where the plain one did not
choices.why: True: the plain one stayed at 2.30 and the residual one fell to a low training loss.

choices.text: Skips work by preventing overfitting
choices.why: They help the optimiser reach a low training loss; overfitting is a different problem.

prompt: A team doubles the input resolution of their EfficientNet-B0 to 448 pixels and keeps everything else. By the lesson's account of compound scaling, what is the likely problem?
hint: What else grows when B-numbers take a larger image?

choices.text: The network refuses an image it was not built for
choices.why: The average pooling before the head accepts any size; it runs.

choices.text: The network is too shallow and narrow for that image
choices.why: Right. A larger image needs more depth and width to cover it; B5 takes 456 pixels with 39 blocks and 512 channels.

choices.text: The parameter count doubles
choices.why: Convolutions do not grow with the image; the parameters stay at 5,288,548 while the work per image grows.

choices.text: It needs pretrained weights at that size first
choices.why: Weights help, but the lesson's point is the shape of the network, not its starting weights.
